title: BarcodeMAE+: Rethinking Masked Pretraining and Global Representations for DNA Barcode Foundation Models
summary: Many DNA foundation models are pretrained by masking parts of a sequence and asking the model to reconstruct them. Standard masked pretraining exposes the encoder to special [MASK] tokens that are absent at inference, creating a mismatch between training and downstream use. The role of an explicit global sequence representation such as a [CLS] token and how it should be trained also remain poorly understood for DNA barcodes. We introduce BarcodeMAE+ and study model architecture, global [CLS] representation, and auxiliary pretraining objectives across arthropod COI (BIOSCAN-5M) and fungal ITS (UNITE+INSD) barcodes. Across both barcode regions, the encoder-decoder MAE-LM architecture outperforms its matched encoder-only counterpart in nearly all evaluated configurations, supporting MAE-LM as an effective architectural design for DNA barcode foundation models. A trained global [CLS] representation provides substantial additional gains: on BIOSCAN-5M, [CLS] accuracy increases from 47.53% without an auxiliary objective to 80.65% with cross-entropy genus classification. The best auxiliary objective is region-dependent: cross-entropy performs best on BIOSCAN-5M, whereas pairwise same-genus classification performs best on UNITE+INSD, reaching 73.19% on Yeast and 63.07% on Filamentous Fungi. BarcodeMAE+ outperforms published DNA foundation model baselines on BIOSCAN-5M and achieves the highest Yeast accuracy among the evaluated UNITE+INSD baselines using frozen encoder representations. Similarity-weighted softmax KNN voting further stabilizes accuracy as neighbourhood size increases. Overall, encoder-decoder masked pretraining and an explicitly trained global representation are strong design choices for DNA barcode foundation models, while the optimal objective for learning that representation depends on the biological domain.

AI.tldr: BarcodeMAE+ studies architecture, global [CLS] representation, and auxiliary objectives for DNA barcode foundation models, finding encoder-decoder masked pretraining (MAE-LM) plus explicitly trained [CLS] gives strong gains, with best auxiliary objective varying by barcode region.
AI.motivation: Standard masked pretraining exposes encoders to [MASK] tokens absent at inference, creating a train/inference mismatch. The role and training of a global [CLS] representation for DNA barcodes is also poorly understood.
AI.method: Introduces BarcodeMAE+ and studies model architecture (encoder-decoder MAE-LM vs encoder-only), global [CLS] representation, and auxiliary pretraining objectives across arthropod COI (BIOSCAN-5M) and fungal ITS (UNITE+INSD) barcodes, including similarity-weighted softmax KNN voting.
AI.result: MAE-LM outperforms encoder-only in nearly all configs. [CLS] accuracy on BIOSCAN-5M rises from 47.53% (no auxiliary) to 80.65% (cross-entropy genus). Best objective is region-dependent: cross-entropy best on BIOSCAN-5M; pairwise same-genus best on UNITE+INSD (73.19% Yeast, 63.07% Filamentous Fungi). BarcodeMAE+ beats DNA foundation baselines on BIOSCAN-5M and tops Yeast accuracy among UNITE+INSD baselines.
AI.conclusion: Encoder-decoder masked pretraining and an explicitly trained global representation are strong design choices for DNA barcode foundation models, but the optimal representation-learning objective is domain-dependent.

title: Failure of the fittest: limits on asexual adaptation to changing environments
summary: The dynamics of adaptation in a population are informed by its mode of reproduction. Whether individuals reproduce sexually or asexually, then, can have large effects on population persistence and extinction in changing environments. Classical theory explains this dependence via genetic variance without further accounting for a fundamentally different mode of inheritance. Recent theoretical advances capture these mechanisms, highlighting how they dramatically change the nature of adaptation in gradually changing environments. Here we show that these recent predictions, which assume infinite-population sizes, are overly optimistic about the fate of finite asexual populations when environmental change is rapid. This is because every individual in an infinite asexual population descends from a once optimal ancestor and the likelihood of finding this optimal individual in the population declines rapidly with population size. To predict the fate of finite asexual populations we derive the equilibrium phenotypic distribution assuming there exist no individuals beyond some unknown trait. As expected, we find that when the phenotypic distribution contains the optimal trait, the population's fate is consistent with previous predictions. When the optimal trait is lost, however, an additional fitness load is incurred. We further derive a prediction for the typical trajectory of an ancestral lineage, which explains the additional load: all individuals descend from a common ancestor carrying the fittest trait, which may be suboptimal. Our work uncovers a finite-population effect that is specific to asexual adaptation and distinct from genetic drift, which significantly hinders the ability of small asexual populations to persist in changing environments.

AI.tldr: Recent predictions about asexual adaptation in changing environments are overly optimistic because they assume infinite populations; finite asexual populations suffer an additional fitness load and persist worse when environmental change is rapid.
AI.motivation: The mode of reproduction (sexual vs asexual) strongly affects population persistence and extinction in changing environments. Recent theory captures how asexual adaptation works in gradually changing environments but relies on infinite-population-size assumptions, leaving the fate of finite asexual populations unclear.
AI.method: The authors derive the equilibrium phenotypic distribution assuming no individuals exist beyond some unknown trait value, and derive a prediction for the typical trajectory of an ancestral lineage to explain the resulting fitness load.
AI.result: When the phenotypic distribution contains the optimal trait, the population's fate matches previous predictions. When the optimal trait is lost, an additional fitness load is incurred, explained by all individuals descending from a common ancestor carrying the fittest (possibly suboptimal) trait.
AI.conclusion: The work uncovers a finite-population effect specific to asexual adaptation, distinct from genetic drift, that significantly hinders small asexual populations from persisting in rapidly changing environments.

title: Better Behavioral Prediction, More Faithful Model Ablations? Evidence from Sequential Choice
summary: Using predictive models to explain cognition requires more than accurate behavioral predictions. Input ablations offer an appealing route: remove information from a model and interpret the resulting performance change as evidence of its importance for behavior. Yet this inference assumes that the model's dependence on information reflects the dependence of the process generating the behavior. We test it in two synthetic sequential bandit tasks with known generating policies, where past choices can remain informative when feedback is unavailable to a predictor. We compare GRUs and Transformers trained from scratch, a fine-tuned LLaMA model, and cognitive models across systematically varied reward contributions. Our analyses distinguish prediction after training without reward observations from the response of a fixed predictor to donor-reward replacement. Three findings emerge. First, in the restless task, neural models trained without rewards predict held-out choices better than four simple training-fitted behavioral baselines. Second, under matched donor replacement, accurate predictors can respond much less than the known generator. Third, at some reward weights, neural networks predict better than a pooled reinforcement-learning model but have less faithful changes in choice probabilities; the model ordering differs between the two tasks. These independent-test results separate information sufficient for prediction from response fidelity under a specified ablation in sequential choice. They motivate validating model-ablation responses independently of predictive performance before using them to infer how the observed behavior was generated.

AI.tldr: Input ablations are commonly used to infer what information a predictive model relies on, but this assumes model dependence mirrors the underlying generative process. In two synthetic sequential bandit tasks, the authors show accurate prediction can dissociate from faithful ablation response, urging independent validation of ablations before inferring behavioral mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Predictive models are increasingly used to explain cognition, and input ablations are an intuitive tool: remove information and read the performance drop as importance. However, this inference is only valid if the model's information dependence matches the dependence of the process that generated the behavior—an assumption rarely tested.
AI.method: Two synthetic sequential bandit tasks with known generating policies, where past choices remain informative even without feedback. Compared GRUs, Transformers trained from scratch, a fine-tuned LLaMA, and cognitive models across systematically varied reward contributions. Two analyses: (1) prediction after training without reward observations, and (2) response of a fixed predictor to donor-reward replacement.
AI.result: Three findings: (1) in the restless task, neural models trained without rewards predict held-out choices better than four training-fitted behavioral baselines; (2) under matched donor replacement, accurate predictors can respond far less than the known generator; (3) at some reward weights, networks predict better than a pooled RL model yet show less faithful choice-probability changes, with model ordering differing across tasks.
AI.conclusion: Information sufficient for prediction is dissociable from response fidelity under a specified ablation in sequential choice. Researchers should validate model-ablation responses independently of predictive performance before using them to infer how observed behavior was generated.

title: Socio-cognitive models in a patch foraging setting: a case study for model selection and parameter identifiability methods
summary: Collective patch-foraging experiments in the laboratory provide a controlled setting in which social information use can be quantified. Here, we consider a go/no-go task in which groups choose between two patches differing in food reward probability. We use agent-based simulations, underpinned by an augmented collective drift-diffusion model, to investigate alternative mechanisms for representing and integrating social information. We consider two representations, continuous (counting representation) and discrete (pulsatile representation), and two integration mechanisms, biasing the decision threshold (threshold modulation) and modifying the accumulated belief (belief modulation), yielding four distinct social models, in addition to a non-interacting model. We first characterize the collective dynamics generated by these models across cognitive parameters and experimental conditions. The temporal dynamics of group accuracy provide informative signatures of the underlying mechanisms. We then assess model selection and parameter identifiability using Bayesian inference and Wasserstein distance minimization, applied to group-accuracy and departure-time distributions. Bayesian inference using distributions of group accuracy provides the most reliable identification across the conditions considered. Importantly, model selection and parameter identifiability are associated with different aspects of collective behavior: model selection is closely linked to the presence of oscillations in the temporal dynamics, whereas parameter identifiability is more closely related to the global accuracy value. Thus, the information available for distinguishing the underlying cognitive mechanisms is not necessarily the same as that required to recover their parameters. Our results further show that identification depends not only on model structure but also on the experimental conditions.

AI.tldr: Agent-based simulations using an augmented collective drift-diffusion model test four social information mechanisms (continuous vs. discrete representation; threshold vs. belief modulation) in a group patch-foraging go/no-go task, finding Bayesian inference on group-accuracy distributions identifies models best, and that model selection and parameter identifiability rely on different behavioral features.
AI.motivation: Laboratory collective patch-foraging experiments offer a controlled way to quantify social information use, but it is unclear which mechanisms for representing and integrating social information underlie group decisions, and how these can be distinguished.
AI.method: Go/no-go task where groups choose between two patches differing in food reward probability. Agent-based simulations built on an augmented collective drift-diffusion model. Two representations (continuous/counting, discrete/pulsatile) crossed with two integration mechanisms (threshold modulation, belief modulation) yield four social models plus a non-interacting model. Model selection and parameter identifiability assessed via Bayesian inference and Wasserstein distance minimization on group-accuracy and departure-time distributions.
AI.result: Temporal dynamics of group accuracy provide signatures of underlying mechanisms. Bayesian inference using group-accuracy distributions gives the most reliable identification across conditions. Model selection links to oscillations in temporal dynamics, while parameter identifiability relates more to global accuracy value. Identification depends on both model structure and experimental conditions.
AI.conclusion: The information distinguishing underlying cognitive mechanisms is not necessarily the same as that needed to recover their parameters; mechanism identification depends on model structure and experimental conditions.

title: Gel-Confined Rolling-Circle Amplification Enables Sensitive Single-Cell Proteoform Analysis
summary: Protein abundance alone does not capture the molecular diversity generated by protein processing and post-translational modification, yet most single-cell protein assays do not resolve these proteoform states. Here, we develop RCAmp-scWB, a post-separation amplification strategy that performs rolling-circle amplification directly within the polyacrylamide gel after single-cell protein electrophoresis. Reaction-transport modeling identifies a balance between reagent access and confinement of the template-associated amplification product that supports signal amplification while retaining the electrophoretically encoded spatial readout. Using purified protein standards, RCAmp-scWB produced a 4.0-7.8-fold steeper concentration-response slope than conventional single-cell western blotting. Across six human cancer cell lines, RCAmp-scWB quantified protein abundance and resolved distinct Vimentin and PD-L1 proteoform states whose relative abundance and single-cell distributions were not captured by total protein measurements alone. Extension to individual small extracellular vesicles further revealed source-dependent shifts in Vimentin proteoform composition despite comparatively similar abundance of one major Vimentin species. By separating electrophoretic molecular discrimination from signal amplification, RCAmp-scWB enables proteoform-resolved analysis of heterogeneous cells and small extracellular vesicles.

AI.tldr: RCAmp-scWB is a post-separation amplification strategy that performs rolling-circle amplification within the gel after single-cell protein electrophoresis, enabling proteoform-resolved single-cell protein analysis.
AI.motivation: Protein abundance alone does not capture molecular diversity from protein processing and post-translational modification, yet most single-cell protein assays fail to resolve these proteoform states.
AI.method: RCAmp-scWB performs rolling-circle amplification directly within the polyacrylamide gel after single-cell protein electrophoresis. Reaction-transport modeling guided a balance between reagent access and confinement of the template-associated amplification product to retain the electrophoretic spatial readout.
AI.result: Using purified standards, RCAmp-scWB produced a 4.0-7.8-fold steeper concentration-response slope than conventional single-cell western blotting. Across six human cancer cell lines, it quantified abundance and resolved distinct Vimentin and PD-L1 proteoform states missed by total protein measurements. It also revealed source-dependent Vimentin proteoform shifts in individual small extracellular vesicles despite similar abundance of a major species.
AI.conclusion: By separating electrophoretic molecular discrimination from signal amplification, RCAmp-scWB enables proteoform-resolved analysis of heterogeneous cells and small extracellular vesicles.

title: Cross-attention encoding models reveal dynamic spatiotemporal routing across human higher visual cortex
summary: Understanding how the brain parses actions and events from time-varying natural inputs is a central challenge in neuroscience. Recent work has used deep neural network (DNN) models to build stimulus-computable fMRI encoding models that predict single-voxel responses to complex natural videos. However, the majority of video-computable encoding models predict responses using simple linear mappings from model tokens, overlooking the spatiotemporal structure shared by video representations and neural responses. Recent cross-attention encoding models address this limitation for static images, enabling flexible stimulus-dependent weighting of image content across space. Here, we extend this framework to naturalistic video, using per-parcel cross-attention to dynamically route features from a self-supervised video model (V-JEPA-2) across both space and time, fitting this model to fMRI responses to short video clips. We compare joint spatiotemporal attention with factorized and selectively constrained alternatives, and find that joint routing improves predictions of brain responses to held-out videos across higher visual regions, most consistently in lateral and dorsal visual areas associated with dynamic motion perception. Moreover, our method provides interpretable, stimulus-specific attention maps that dynamically follow moving objects, revealing which locations and temporal moments contribute to each neural response. We further show that attention maps from parcels in different category-selective networks (face-, body-, scene-selective) differentially weight content in accordance with expected semantic selectivity. Together, this work provides a new computational framework for understanding how visual information is adaptively weighted by cortical populations during dynamic visual perception.

AI.tldr: The paper extends cross-attention fMRI encoding models to naturalistic video by using per-parcel cross-attention over a self-supervised video model (V-JEPA-2) to route features across space and time.
AI.motivation: Most video-computable fMRI encoding models rely on simple linear mappings from model tokens, ignoring the spatiotemporal structure shared between video representations and neural responses. Cross-attention has helped for static images but has not been extended to video.
AI.method: Per-parcel cross-attention that dynamically routes features from V-JEPA-2 across space and time, fitted to fMRI responses to short video clips. Joint spatiotemporal attention is compared with factorized and selectively constrained alternatives.
AI.result: Joint routing improves prediction of held-out video responses across higher visual regions, most consistently in lateral and dorsal areas tied to dynamic motion perception. Attention maps follow moving objects and reveal contributing locations/moments; parcels in face-, body-, and scene-selective networks differentially weight content matching expected semantic selectivity.
AI.conclusion: A new computational framework for understanding how cortical populations adaptively weight visual information during dynamic visual perception.

title: Receptive-field-constrained stimulus optimization for human early and intermediate visual cortex
summary: An ongoing challenge in sensory neuroscience is to characterize the feature dimensions encoded by cortical populations. Recent approaches probe feature selectivity in a data-driven way, by synthesizing a most-exciting-input (MEI) for a target neural population. While this approach has been successfully applied to human higher visual cortex using fMRI data, generating MEIs for early- and mid-level retinotopic visual areas requires additional modeling constraints due to small receptive field sizes. To address this challenge, we introduce two novel MEI generation frameworks, Receptive Field Diffusion for Visual Exploration (RF-DiVE) and Receptive Field Gradient Optimization (RF-GO). Both methods use a population receptive field (pRF)-constrained voxelwise encoding model; RF-DiVE combines this with a pretrained latent diffusion model, while RF-GO uses regularized gradient ascent. When applied to single voxels in retinotopically defined areas V1-hV4, using data from the Natural Scenes Dataset, we obtain MEIs that exhibit consistent structure within the pRF, suggesting selectivity for local features like contour, color, and texture. We systematically compare MEIs generated by RF-DiVE and RF-GO using two encoding backbones, performing in-silico validation of predicted responses to MEIs using independent encoding models. Across all methods and all visual areas, MEIs elicit higher model-predicted responses than the most activating natural images. We further find that the choice of generation framework and encoding backbone differentially affects MEI properties, including their visual appearance, structural interpretability, and cross-model generalizability. These results offer a new approach for performing data-driven characterization of spatial and feature selectivity across human visual cortex.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces RF-DiVE and RF-GO, two pRF-constrained methods to generate most-exciting-inputs (MEIs) for early- and mid-level human retinotopic visual areas (V1-hV4), where small receptive fields make standard MEI synthesis difficult.
AI.motivation: Characterizing feature dimensions encoded by cortical populations is a key challenge in sensory neuroscience. Data-driven MEI synthesis works well for higher visual cortex with fMRI, but fails in early/mid-level retinotopic areas because of small receptive field sizes, requiring additional modeling constraints.
AI.method: Two novel MEI generation frameworks: RF-DiVE (combines a pRF-constrained voxelwise encoding model with a pretrained latent diffusion model) and RF-GO (uses regularized gradient ascent). Applied to single voxels in retinotopically defined areas V1-hV4 using Natural Scenes Dataset, with two encoding backbones and in-silico validation via independent encoding models.
AI.result: MEIs exhibit consistent structure within the pRF, suggesting selectivity for local features like contour, color, and texture. Across all methods and visual areas, MEIs elicit higher model-predicted responses than the most activating natural images. Generation framework and encoding backbone differentially affect MEI visual appearance, structural interpretability, and cross-model generalizability.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approaches offer a new way to perform data-driven characterization of spatial and feature selectivity across human visual cortex.

title: Where Should Physics Enter a Molecular Crystal Generator?
summary: Generative models make molecular crystal structure prediction fast, but their samples still exhibit geometric and packing violations. Physics can be introduced during training, post-training, or inference, yet these choices are rarely compared with the generator and physical signal held fixed. We introduce CrystAF, an all-atom crystal flow-map generation model, and use it with the UMA interatomic potential to systematically study where physics should enter. Post-training learns physical preferences directly into CrystAF, improving molecular validity and crystal packing while leaving sampling unchanged: physics is paid for once during training rather than repeatedly at deployment. In contrast, UMA relaxation is effective at repairing local clashes but makes generation 6--26$\times$ slower, while learning from relaxed targets provides little benefit. These routes are complementary rather than competing. Physics-informed post-training first shifts the generated distribution toward more physically reasonable structures, after which inexpensive inference-time corrections further remove clashes and restore stereochemistry that the generator cannot represent. Importantly, the same post-training strategy also improves the multi-step all-atom Clari-M and rigid-body MolCrystalFlow generators, demonstrating transfer across architectures and representations. Together, our results suggest a simple principle: learn reusable physical alignment into the generator, and reserve inference-time physics for residual constraints that are better corrected than learned.

AI.tldr: CrystAF, an all-atom crystal flow-map model, is used with the UMA interatomic potential to systematically compare where physics should enter crystal structure prediction: during training (post-training), post-training-from-relaxed-targets, or inference (relaxation). Physics-informed post-training integrates physical preferences into the generator at low cost and transfers across architectures, while inference-time relaxation is best reserved for residual constraints.
AI.motivation: Generative models make molecular crystal structure prediction fast, but their samples still exhibit geometric and packing violations. Physics can be introduced at various stages, yet these choices are rarely compared with the generator and physical signal held fixed.
AI.method: Introduces CrystAF, an all-atom crystal flow-map generation model, paired with the UMA interatomic potential. Systematically compares three physics-injection routes: (1) physics-informed post-training that learns physical preferences directly into the generator, (2) inference-time UMA relaxation, and (3) learning from relaxed targets. The post-training strategy is also applied to Clari-M (multi-step all-atom) and MolCrystalFlow (rigid-body) generators.
AI.result: Post-training improves molecular validity and crystal packing while leaving sampling unchanged, paying the physics cost once at training rather than repeatedly at deployment. UMA relaxation repairs local clashes but slows generation 6--26x, and learning from relaxed targets provides little benefit. The same post-training strategy also improves Clari-M and MolCrystalFlow, showing transfer across architectures and representations.
AI.conclusion: The routes are complementary rather than competing: physics-informed post-training first shifts the generated distribution toward more physically reasonable structures, after which inexpensive inference-time corrections remove residual clashes and restore stereochemistry. The simple principle suggested is to learn reusable physical alignment into the generator and reserve inference-time physics for residual constraints better corrected than learned.

title: The Fluid Mechanics of Truncus Arteriosus
summary: Truncus arteriosus (TA) is a rare, severe congenital heart disease in which the two main arteries exiting the heart fail to separate in utero resulting in one truncus and truncal valve, carrying mixed oxygenated and deoxygenated blood. About 25% of patients have a quadricuspid valve, which is prone to regurgitation and re-intervention. Despite its relevance for valve performance and mixing, fluid mechanics in TA are poorly understood. Patient-specific fluid-structure interaction simulations were performed based on CT imaging before and after TA repair. The quadricuspid valve was constructed using elasticity-based design with the patient's free edge length and geometric height extracted from echocardiography. Interaction between blood and valve was simulated with the Immersed Boundary Method. Boundary conditions were tuned to the patient's data. Mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood and streaming were assessed via Lagrangian Coherent Structures (LCS) and Lagrangian Particle Tracing (LPT). Low pressures, forward flow and streamwise vortices in the one-sided pulmonary arteries (PAs) throughout the cardiac cycle affected leaflet motion, leading to asymmetric closure and regurgitation. Holodiastolic aortic flow reversal supplied PA flow and the regurgitant jet. LCS and LPT indicated favorable streaming of oxygenated blood from the LV to the aorta and deoxygenated blood from the RV to the PAs. After truncal surgery, normal hemodynamics were restored. This is the first study of fluid mechanics of TA. Using qualitative and quantitative flow analysis, we identified disrupted preoperative hemodynamics caused by one-sided PAs and showed how normal hemodynamics were re-established after repair. Favorable streaming was demonstrated aligned with patient reports. Thus, favorable streaming is plausible in total mixing lesions and patient-specific modeling may aid in its detection.

AI.tldr: First patient-specific fluid-structure interaction study of truncus arteriosus (TA), revealing disrupted preoperative hemodynamics from one-sided pulmonary arteries and showing normal hemodynamics restored after repair.
AI.motivation: TA is a rare severe congenital heart disease with a single truncus and truncal valve carrying mixed blood. About 25% of patients have a quadricuspid valve prone to regurgitation and re-intervention. Despite its importance for valve performance and blood mixing, TA fluid mechanics remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Patient-specific fluid-structure interaction simulations based on pre- and post-repair CT imaging. A quadricuspid valve was constructed with elasticity-based design using patient free edge length and geometric height from echocardiography. Blood-valve interaction was simulated via the Immersed Boundary Method, with patient-tuned boundary conditions. Mixing and streaming were assessed using Lagrangian Coherent Structures (LCS) and Lagrangian Particle Tracing (LPT).
AI.result: Low pressures, forward flow, and streamwise vortices in one-sided pulmonary arteries caused asymmetric leaflet motion, asymmetric closure, and regurgitation. Holodiastolic aortic flow reversal supplied PA flow and the regurgitant jet. LCS and LPT showed favorable streaming: oxygenated blood from LV to aorta and deoxygenated blood from RV to PAs. After surgery, normal hemodynamics were restored.
AI.conclusion: This is the first study of TA fluid mechanics. Qualitative and quantitative flow analysis identified disrupted preoperative hemodynamics caused by one-sided PAs, showed normal hemodynamics re-established after repair, and demonstrated favorable streaming consistent with patient reports. Patient-specific modeling may aid in detecting favorable streaming in total mixing lesions.

title: RNA Design via Conditioned Flow Matching and Finite-Policy Reinforcement Learning
summary: RNA design aims to identify sequences that fold into specified secondary structures. Existing methods formulate the task as target-specific search or conditional generation. However, natural RNA evolution proceeds through sequence variation and selection, with compensatory substitutions, whereas these methods do not explicitly model this process. To address this limitation, we propose a two-stage framework comprising RNA Inverse-Folding Flow (RNA-IFlow) and RNA-IFlow-RL. RNA-IFlow uses structure-conditioned Dirichlet Flow Matching to model coordinated variation across the sequence, while RNA-IFlow-RL maps the learned flow to a pairing-preserving finite policy and refines it with thermodynamic feedback. Our framework achieves leading performance on multiple benchmarks, reaching 85.19% Pass@1 on Rfam-27. Further analyses reveal thermodynamic gains, policy dynamics, and robustness across settings. Our work couples coordinated variation with thermodynamic selection, offering a novel paradigm for RNA design.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RNA-IFlow and RNA-IFlow-RL, a two-stage framework that models RNA design as structure-conditioned Dirichlet Flow Matching followed by reinforcement learning refinement with thermodynamic feedback, achieving state-of-the-art results including 85.19% Pass@1 on Rfam-27.
AI.motivation: Existing RNA design methods use target-specific search or conditional generation, but fail to explicitly model natural RNA evolution, which proceeds via sequence variation and selection with compensatory substitutions.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) RNA-IFlow uses structure-conditioned Dirichlet Flow Matching to model coordinated sequence variation; (2) RNA-IFlow-RL maps the learned flow to a pairing-preserving finite policy refined via thermodynamic feedback.
AI.result: Leading performance on multiple benchmarks, reaching 85.19% Pass@1 on Rfam-27, with further analyses showing thermodynamic gains, policy dynamics, and robustness across settings.
AI.conclusion: By coupling coordinated variation with thermodynamic selection, the work offers a novel paradigm for RNA design that better mirrors natural RNA evolution.

title: An adaptive fractional state links circuit mechanisms to cortical dynamics across the visual hierarchy
comment: 47 pages (41 main + 6 supplementary), 4 figures, 1 table, 4 supplementary figures, 1 supplementary video (ancillary file). Code: https://github.com/brendanjohnharris/WorkingRegime.jl
summary: Cortical circuits must respond flexibly to new inputs while integrating information about the past, yet the way in which neural activity reconciles these competing demands remains unclear. Combining Neuropixels recordings from six mouse visual areas with mechanistic circuit modeling, we identify a dynamical regime in which heavy-tailed superdiffusive fluctuations coexist with long-range temporal dependence and oscillations. We formalize this regime as the adaptive fractional (AF) state, using an effective mean-field theory in which spatial and temporal fractional derivatives capture heavy-tailed excursions and long-range memory, respectively. We find that dynamical exponents characterizing the AF state vary systematically across the visual hierarchy: higher visual areas exhibit weaker superdiffusion and stronger temporal memory. In the circuit model, this hierarchical shift emerges from a progressive weakening of effective inhibition. These findings extend the classical hierarchy of timescales to a hierarchy of dynamical regimes and suggest that the AF state allows cortical areas to jointly express rapid responses and long-term temporal integration.

AI.tldr: Combining Neuropixels recordings from six mouse visual areas with circuit modeling, the paper identifies an "adaptive fractional (AF) state" where heavy-tailed superdiffusion coexists with long-range temporal memory and oscillations, changing systematically across the visual hierarchy.
AI.motivation: Cortical circuits must respond flexibly to new inputs while integrating past information, but how neural activity reconciles these competing demands (rapid response vs. long-term integration) remains unclear.
AI.method: Neuropixels recordings from six mouse visual areas combined with a mechanistic circuit model and an effective mean-field theory using spatial and temporal fractional derivatives to capture heavy-tailed excursions and long-range memory.
AI.result: The AF state shows heavy-tailed superdiffusive fluctuations coexisting with long-range temporal dependence and oscillations. Dynamical exponents vary systematically across the visual hierarchy: higher visual areas exhibit weaker superdiffusion and stronger temporal memory. In the circuit model, this hierarchical shift emerges from progressive weakening of effective inhibition.
AI.conclusion: The findings extend the classical hierarchy of timescales to a hierarchy of dynamical regimes, suggesting the AF state lets cortical areas jointly express rapid responses and long-term temporal integration.

title: Leveraging secondary-structure information for accurate nucleic acid structure prediction with OFoldNA
summary: Recent advances in biomolecular structure prediction have enabled accurate modelling of increasingly complex molecular systems. However, nucleic acid structure prediction remains challenging because of conformational flexibility and the limited availability of high-quality 3D structural data. Secondary structure (SS) provides a more readily available layer of structural information that captures base-pairing relationships and folding topology. Here we present OFoldNA, an all-atom diffusion model that incorporates SS information into nucleic acid folding and protein--nucleic acid co-folding. Without external SS information, OFoldNA achieved leading performance on FoldBench for both nucleic acid monomer folding and protein--nucleic acid co-folding, with particularly strong performance on DNA monomers and protein--DNA interfaces involving longer nucleic acid chains. When accurate base-pairing information was provided, OFoldNA-SS2TS further improved both folding and co-folding accuracy, while partial SS information also yielded consistent gains. The same auxiliary branch can also be used for RNA SS prediction as OFoldNA-SS, which achieved the best out-of-distribution performance on CHANRG. Together, these results show that intermediate structural information such as nucleic acid SS can be leveraged to improve all-atom 3D modelling, providing a general direction for incorporating complementary structural modalities into molecular structure prediction and design.

AI.tldr: OFoldNA is an all-atom diffusion model that integrates secondary structure (SS) information to improve nucleic acid folding and protein-nucleic acid co-folding, achieving leading performance and demonstrating that SS can enhance 3D structure prediction.
AI.motivation: Nucleic acid structure prediction remains challenging due to conformational flexibility and limited high-quality 3D structural data, whereas secondary structure offers more readily available base-pairing and folding topology information.
AI.method: OFoldNA is an all-atom diffusion model incorporating SS information into nucleic acid folding and protein-nucleic acid co-folding. An auxiliary branch supports RNA SS prediction (OFoldNA-SS), and a variant (OFoldNA-SS2TS) uses accurate base-pairing information.
AI.result: Without external SS, OFoldNA achieved leading FoldBench performance, especially for DNA monomers and protein-DNA interfaces with longer chains. With accurate base-pairing (OFoldNA-SS2TS), folding and co-folding accuracy improved further, and partial SS also yielded consistent gains. OFoldNA-SS achieved the best out-of-distribution performance on CHANRG.
AI.conclusion: Intermediate structural information such as nucleic acid SS can be leveraged to improve all-atom 3D modelling, offering a general direction for incorporating complementary structural modalities into molecular structure prediction and design.

title: How 'Foundational' Are Current Molecular Foundation Models?
summary: Large-scale models have permeated the molecular sciences, yet what makes a model 'foundational' in this domain remains poorly defined. This paper proposes three testable criteria for assessing the foundational nature of molecular models: (i) generality across molecular entities, properties, and tasks; (ii) transferability to new applications with no or minimal task-specific retraining; and (iii) generalization beyond the training distribution. Applying these criteria to the state of the art reveals promising progress, particularly visible in biomolecular structure prediction and machine-learned interatomic potentials, although none of the approaches examined fully satisfies all three. Success is concentrated in domains where target properties are consistently defined and training data are abundant, with low label noise relative to physically meaningful variation. More broadly, progress in the molecular sciences appears to depend less on model scale alone than on the quality and structure of available data, as well as the incorporation of prior knowledge into models, prediction tasks, or downstream applications. This work shifts the notion of a molecular foundation model from a descriptive label to a testable hypothesis, offering a framework for assessing current models and guiding future developments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes three testable criteria for defining molecular foundation models—generality, transferability, and generalization—and applies them to current state-of-the-art approaches.
AI.motivation: Large-scale models have spread through the molecular sciences, but what makes a model 'foundational' in this domain remains poorly defined, motivating the need for a concrete, testable framework.
AI.method: The authors define three criteria: (i) generality across molecular entities, properties, and tasks; (ii) transferability to new applications with no or minimal task-specific retraining; and (iii) generalization beyond the training distribution. They apply these criteria to state-of-the-art models.
AI.result: Application reveals promising progress, notably in biomolecular structure prediction and machine-learned interatomic potentials, though no approach fully satisfies all three criteria. Success concentrates where target properties are consistently defined and training data are abundant with low label noise relative to physically meaningful variation.
AI.conclusion: Progress in molecular sciences depends less on model scale than on data quality and structure and the incorporation of prior knowledge. The work reframes the molecular foundation model from a descriptive label to a testable hypothesis, offering a framework to assess current models and guide future work.

title: Stochastic gradient descent on the epigenetic landscape: a unified framework for cellular plasticity, tumor heterogeneity, and the asymptotic irrelevance of fitness
summary: Phenotypic plasticity, the ability of cells to switch between states, is central to development, differentiation, and therapy resistance. Although it is modeled at several scales, from compartmental ODEs to phenotype-structured PDEs and single-cell stochastic equations, a framework connecting these descriptions is missing. We present such a framework. Starting from a general $n$-compartment ODE model encompassing nonlinear growth and linear transitions between phenotypes, we show, with a new, elementary and generalizable proof of a recent theorem, that under uniform competition, the long-term population distribution is solely governed by transition rates. All phenotypes become selectively neutral at saturation, and the imprint of fitness differences during growth fades at an explicit rate. Restricting transitions to neighboring states transforms the model into a discretization of a phenotype-structured reaction-diffusion-advection PDE. In this continuum model, diffusion and advection are identified from switching rates, and fitness remains asymptotically irrelevant. Interpreting the advection velocity as the negative gradient of an effective epigenetic potential transforms the PDE into a Fokker--Planck equation and converts single-cell trajectories into stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in the Langevin sense on the phenotypic landscape. Non-local transitions, such as mutations, are incorporated via an integro-differential term, yielding a unified model with reaction, gradient flow, diffusion, and jumps. State-dependent noise reshapes the effective landscape without altering the underlying potential. This gives cancer a route to elevated plasticity that static, single-cell snapshots cannot distinguish from a changed landscape. This framework provides a physical interpretation of Waddington's landscape, where cells perform SGD, and cancer corresponds to a corrupted landscape.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unifying multiscale framework connecting compartmental ODEs, phenotype-structured PDEs, and single-cell stochastic equations for phenotypic plasticity, showing transition rates govern long-term distributions and linking this to Waddington's landscape and cancer plasticity.
AI.motivation: Phenotypic plasticity—cells switching between states—is central to development, differentiation, and therapy resistance, and is modeled across many scales (ODE, PDE, stochastic). However, no framework connects these separate descriptions, leaving the relationships between them unclear.
AI.method: Starting from a general n-compartment ODE model with nonlinear growth and linear transitions, they give a new, elementary, generalizable proof of a recent theorem. Restricting transitions to neighboring states yields a discretization of a phenotype-structured reaction-diffusion-advection PDE. Interpreting advection as the negative gradient of an effective epigenetic potential converts this into a Fokker-Planck equation, linking single-cell trajectories to SGD in the Langevin sense. Non-local transitions (mutations) add an integro-differential term, giving a unified reaction-gradient-flow-diffusion-jump model.
