In the continuum model, diffusion and advection derive from switching rates and fitness is asymptotically irrelevant. State-dependent noise reshapes the effective landscape without altering the potential, giving cancer a route to elevated plasticity indistinguishable from a changed landscape in static single-cell snapshots.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a physical interpretation of Waddington's landscape where cells perform stochastic gradient descent, and cancer corresponds to a corrupted landscape.

title: CancerZigZag: Iterative Seed-Anchored Diffusion for Generative Modeling of Single-Cell State Transitions
comment: 26 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Accepted for oral presentation at ISCB-AI 2026
summary: Single-cell cancer datasets are predominantly cross-sectional and rarely provide paired or longitudinal observations linking individual healthy-like cells to tumor-associated states. We introduce CancerZigZag, a seed-initialized diffusion-based framework for exploratory generation of tumor-associated single-cell candidate clouds from unpaired epithelial cell populations. For each cancer context, a diffusion model is trained exclusively on tumor-derived epithelial cells and applied through repeated partial latent-space perturbation and reverse diffusion to held-out healthy-like seeds, generating stochastic candidate clouds without paired measurements or classifier guidance. We applied CancerZigZag to colorectal, breast, lung, and renal cell carcinoma contexts and explored parameter landscapes defined by perturbation depth and the number of ZigZag cycles. Across the reported operating configurations, candidate clouds contained outputs classified toward held-out tumor-derived reference populations for each evaluated seed. Residual seed-dependent organization varied across contexts, with the clearest structure in colorectal cancer, more modest organization in lung cancer, and limited cloud-level structure in breast and renal cell carcinoma. Representative candidates also showed directional concordance with transcriptional shifts observed between held-out healthy-like and tumor-derived reference populations. CancerZigZag is not interpreted as a model of deterministic healthy-to-tumor transformation or cellular progression. Instead, it provides a reference-informed framework for exploring tumor-associated candidate distributions from unpaired healthy-like seeds and quantifying the context-dependent relationship between tumor-associated displacement and residual seed dependence.

AI.tldr: CancerZigZag is a seed-initialized diffusion framework that generates tumor-associated single-cell candidate clouds from unpaired healthy-like epithelial cells, using tumor-trained diffusion with repeated latent perturbation and reverse diffusion.
AI.motivation: Single-cell cancer datasets are mostly cross-sectional and rarely provide paired or longitudinal observations linking healthy-like cells to tumor-associated states, limiting direct study of tumor-associated shifts.
AI.method: Train a diffusion model exclusively on tumor-derived epithelial cells per cancer context, then apply repeated partial latent-space perturbation and reverse diffusion to held-out healthy-like seeds to generate stochastic candidate clouds, without paired measurements or classifier guidance. Explored parameter landscapes defined by perturbation depth and number of ZigZag cycles.
AI.result: Applied to colorectal, breast, lung, and renal cell carcinoma. Candidate clouds contained outputs classified toward held-out tumor-derived reference populations for each evaluated seed. Residual seed-dependent organization varied: clearest in colorectal, modest in lung, limited in breast and renal. Representative candidates showed directional concordance with transcriptional shifts between held-out healthy-like and tumor-derived references.
AI.conclusion: CancerZigZag is not a model of deterministic healthy-to-tumor transformation or progression, but a reference-informed framework for exploring tumor-associated candidate distributions from unpaired healthy-like seeds and quantifying context-dependent displacement versus residual seed dependence.

title: Nutrient Competition as a General Mechanism of Regulation in Photosymbiosis
summary: Nitrogen limitation is a key mechanism regulating the mutualism between photosymbiotic cnidarians and their algal symbionts. Algal-derived photosynthate facilitates host assimilation of inorganic nitrogen, specifically ammonium. The resulting competition between symbiotic partners for inorganic nitrogen leads to a negative feedback loop wherein symbiont density is effectively controlled through facilitation of their competitor. However, it is unclear whether this feedback loop is sufficient to stabilize the interaction absent other forms of regulation. Using a generalized modeling approach, we identify the conditions under which cnidarian-algal competition for nitrogen yields dynamically stable symbioses. We show that nitrogen limitation is sufficient to stabilize the interaction through the interplay of intraspecific (symbiont-symbiont) and interspecific (host-symbiont) competition. As host assimilation of inorganic nitrogen increases, the system shifts from being stabilized by intraspecific competition between symbionts to interspecific competition between host and symbionts, necessitating a positive coupling of symbiont density to host nitrogen assimilation via photosynthate translocation for dynamic stability.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a generalized modeling approach to show that nitrogen limitation alone can stabilize cnidarian-algal symbioses through interplay of intra- and interspecific competition.
AI.motivation: Nitrogen limitation is thought to regulate cnidarian-algal mutualism via a negative feedback loop, but it was unclear whether this feedback alone suffices to stabilize the interaction without other regulatory mechanisms.
AI.method: A generalized modeling approach is used to analyze cnidarian-algal competition for inorganic nitrogen and identify conditions yielding dynamically stable symbioses.
AI.result: Nitrogen limitation is sufficient to stabilize the interaction via interplay of intraspecific (symbiont-symbiont) and interspecific (host-symbiont) competition. As host assimilation of inorganic nitrogen increases, stabilization shifts from intraspecific to interspecific competition, requiring positive coupling of symbiont density to host nitrogen assimilation via photosynthate translocation.
AI.conclusion: Nitrogen limitation can by itself stabilize photosymbiotic cnidarian-algal mutualism, with the stabilizing competition mode depending on the level of host nitrogen assimilation.

title: Boids of a Feather Flock Together - Evolving Prey Behaviours Under Different Predator Attack Strategies
summary: Flocking and schooling are thought to have evolved partly as defences against predation, but how prey should balance social and escape tendencies may depend on the predator's hunting strategy. We extend the predator-prey boids model of Ojo et al. (2023), itself based on Reynolds' boids, by combining six prey movement tendencies (alignment, cohesion, separation, dodge, repel and wiggle) into a single weighted acceleration update, and by reformulating wiggle as a sinusoidal manoeuvre. We then use an evolutionary strategy to optimise the six behaviour coefficients for collective prey survival against four predator hunting strategies: attack-centroid, attack-nearest, attack-random and attack-peripheral. Across five independent trials per strategy, coefficients converged within trials and mean fitness remained stable or increased, although trials often settled in different local optima. Prey survival was highest under attack-centroid and lowest under attack-nearest, in line with our hypotheses. Against attack-centroid, prey evolved individualistic predator avoidance with high escape coefficients, whereas against the other three strategies they largely kept their flock formation. Across all strategies, evolution favoured a low repel coefficient and relatively high dodge and wiggle coefficients. Our results suggest that optimal anti-predator behaviour depends on the interplay between escape tendencies and the predator's hunting strategy.

AI.tldr: Extending the Ojo et al. (2023) predator-prey boids model, the authors combine six prey movement tendencies into one weighted acceleration update and use an evolutionary strategy to optimize behavior coefficients against four predator hunting strategies, finding that optimal anti-predator behavior depends on the interaction between escape tendencies and the predator's hunting strategy.
AI.motivation: Flocking and schooling are believed to have evolved partly as defenses against predation, but how prey should balance social versus escape tendencies likely depends on the predator's hunting strategy. This motivates testing how prey behavior evolves under different predator tactics.
AI.method: The authors extend the predator-prey boids model of Ojo et al. (2023), based on Reynolds' boids, by combining six prey movement tendencies (alignment, cohesion, separation, dodge, repel, and wiggle) into a single weighted acceleration update, and reformulating wiggle as a sinusoidal maneuver. An evolutionary strategy optimizes the six behavior coefficients for collective prey survival against four predator hunting strategies: attack-centroid, attack-nearest, attack-random, and attack-peripheral, with five independent trials per strategy.
AI.result: Coefficients converged within trials and mean fitness remained stable or increased, though trials often settled in different local optima. Prey survival was highest under attack-centroid and lowest under attack-nearest, matching the hypotheses. Against attack-centroid, prey evolved individualistic avoidance with high escape coefficients; against the other three strategies, they largely maintained flock formation. Evolution favored a low repel coefficient and relatively high dodge and wiggle coefficients across all strategies.
AI.conclusion: Optimal anti-predator behavior depends on the interplay between escape tendencies and the predator's hunting strategy, indicating that prey should adapt their balance of social and escape behaviors to the specific threat.

title: GenoTrace: Inheritable Watermarks for Genome Foundation Model Distillation
summary: Can a genome model retain a detectable record of the synthetic sequences used to train it? We study watermark inheritance through distillation with GenoTrace, a codon-aware extension of green-list watermarking. Two token-level factors modulate the teacher's generation bias using codon position and organism-specific codon usage. The resulting sequences train a smaller student, whose outputs are audited without an active watermark processor. In a three-seed GenomeOcean-500M-to-100M experiment, the joint configuration achieves a mean audit score of 17.88 and 94.5% detection at a fixed threshold. It retains 49.0% detection after key-aware token substitution, compared with 0% for the available single-seed plain-watermark comparator, and 47.0% after combined mechanism-targeted nucleotide edits. Additional experiments establish inherited signal across five organism-conditioned datasets and teacher-student size ratios up to 40. Component ablations and computational sequence-quality assays reveal distinct operating points for detection strength and coding coverage. GenoTrace provides a practical token-level construction and an empirical account of how genomic structure shapes inherited watermark signals. The findings concern shared-tokenizer distillation and the tested editing procedures, with calibration and biological utility treated as separate evaluation requirements.

AI.tldr: GenoTrace, a codon-aware green-list watermarking method, enables synthetic sequence watermarks to be inherited through teacher-student distillation in genome models, retaining detection even under token substitution and nucleotide edits.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether a genome model can retain a detectable record of the synthetic sequences used to train it, motivating watermark inheritance tracking through distillation for provenance and accountability.
AI.method: GenoTrace extends green-list watermarking with codon awareness, using codon position and organism-specific codon usage as two token-level factors to modulate the teacher's generation bias. A smaller student is distilled on these sequences and audited without an active watermark processor, tested across three seeds, five organism-conditioned datasets, and size ratios up to 40, plus component ablations and sequence-quality assays.
AI.result: In GenomeOcean-500M-to-100M experiments, the joint configuration reaches a mean audit score of 17.88 and 94.5% detection at a fixed threshold. It retains 49.0% detection after key-aware token substitution (vs. 0% for the plain-watermark comparator) and 47.0% after combined mechanism-targeted nucleotide edits.
AI.conclusion: GenoTrace offers a practical token-level construction and empirical insight into how genomic structure shapes inherited watermark signals. Findings apply to shared-tokenizer distillation and tested edits, with calibration and biological utility as separate evaluation needs.

title: GenomeOcean Anywhere: Private WebGPU Inference for Genome MoEs
summary: Genome foundation models are most useful where sequences are generated, yet the largest models need datacenter accelerators and a place to send private DNA. We ask whether a 15-billion-parameter genome mixture-of-experts (MoE) model can instead run on volunteers' web browsers, with the experts spread across many untrusted devices, without changing its predictions and without revealing the sequence to any single device. We build a system in which a trusted coordinator runs attention and routing while browser workers run every expert feed-forward network through hand-written WebGPU kernels, and we protect the expert inputs with real-valued Lagrange coded computing: each worker receives only a Gaussian-padded share, computes the expert's linear maps, and the coordinator decodes from any two of three workers. On GenomeOcean-MoE (8 experts, top-2 routing, 24 layers), the browser path matches native llama.cpp at every quantization level, the distributed path stays at the BF16 numerical noise floor (KL 0.0036 nats per token), and an unfitted latency model predicts decode time within 0.74% (median) under emulated wide-area links. We first show that plaintext expert inputs are not private: a probe recovers the token from a single vector at every depth, and one worker can identify the source genome from 300 unordered tokens with 92% accuracy. With coded experts, an adaptive attacker trained on shares falls to the most-frequent-token baseline, one worker's information about each token is bounded below one bit per forward pass, and the fidelity cost stays below the BF16 noise floor; in Chrome, coded decoding runs at 220 to 376 ms per token, depending on how much of the routing is hidden, and continues without replicas when a worker fails.

AI.tldr: A 15B-parameter genome MoE model runs distributed across volunteers' web browsers using WebGPU kernels and Lagrange coded computing, matching native llama.cpp outputs and BF16 precision while preventing any single untrusted device from recovering the private DNA sequence.
AI.motivation: Genome foundation models are most useful where sequences are generated, but the largest models require datacenter accelerators and force users to send private DNA to a central server. The authors ask whether a large genome MoE model can instead run on volunteers' browsers, with experts spread across untrusted devices, without changing predictions or leaking the sequence.
AI.method: A trusted coordinator runs attention and routing while browser workers execute every expert feed-forward network via hand-written WebGPU kernels. Expert inputs are protected with real-valued Lagrange coded computing: each worker gets only a Gaussian-padded share, computes the expert's linear maps, and the coordinator decodes from any two of three workers (tolerating one failure without replicas). Evaluated on GenomeOcean-MoE (8 experts, top-2 routing, 24 layers).
AI.result: Browser path matches native llama.cpp at every quantization level; distributed path stays at the BF16 noise floor (KL 0.0036 nats/token); an unfitted latency model predicts decode time within 0.74% median under emulated WAN links. Privacy: plaintext inputs leak (a probe recovers the token from a single vector at every depth; one worker identifies the source genome from 300 unordered tokens with 92% accuracy). With coded experts, an adaptive attacker drops to the most-frequent-token baseline, per-token information is bounded below one bit per forward pass, and fidelity cost stays below the BF16 noise floor. In Chrome, coded decoding runs at 220–376 ms/token.
AI.conclusion: A privacy-preserving, fault-tolerant browser-based inference system can run a 15B genome MoE model at near-native fidelity, keeping raw DNA off any single device while delivering practical latency and resilience to worker failure.

title: CipherGenome: Homomorphic Inference for Genomic Mixture-of-Experts
summary: Genome foundation models are growing into sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) networks whose expert weights no longer fit on the machines that hold the sequences, yet sending a private genome to rented accelerators exposes it: we show that a single server hosting one expert recovers the input nucleotides with 99.8% top-1 accuracy. We present CipherGenome, a protocol that keeps the embedding, attention and router of a 15.1B-parameter MoE genome model on a trusted thin client and outsources every expert projection, 95.8% of the parameters, to untrusted and possibly colluding GPU servers under module-LWE encryption. The design exploits three structural facts: expert layers are linear between two SwiGLU gates, expert weights are public, and GPU integer tensor cores can evaluate a ciphertext-weight product exactly modulo $2^{48}$ in a single GEMM. The client evaluates the nonlinearity exactly and re-encrypts with fresh secrets, so no polynomial approximation or bootstrapping is ever needed. On 72 windows from 12 bacterial genomes, encryption adds $2.54 \times 10^{-4}$ nats per token of KL divergence (95% CI upper bound $3.95 \times 10^{-4}$), below a pre-registered non-inferiority margin and indistinguishable from bf16 inference, while the same inversion attack falls to chance level. A reusable public hint cuts end-to-end latency by 3.54 times, wire compression reduces traffic 6.8 times, per-layer padding reduces routing leakage from 54.9% to 8.9% accuracy, and HE-compatible int4 experts remain non-inferior to their plaintext counterparts. Per expert and token, the server-side cost is more than six orders of magnitude below a CKKS baseline.

AI.tldr: CipherGenome is a protocol that keeps a 15.1B-parameter MoE genome model's embedding, attention, and router on a trusted client while outsourcing expert projections (95.8% of parameters) to untrusted GPUs under module-LWE encryption, achieving bf16-comparable accuracy with negligible KL divergence and defeating inversion attacks.
AI.motivation: Genome foundation models increasingly use sparse MoE networks too large to fit on client machines, but outsourcing private genome data to rented accelerators exposes the input—a single server holding one expert can recover input nucleotides with 99.8% top-1 accuracy.
AI.method: CipherGenome keeps embedding, attention, and router on a trusted thin client and outsources expert projections to untrusted, possibly colluding GPU servers under module-LWE encryption. It exploits three facts: expert layers are linear between two SwiGLU gates, expert weights are public, and GPU integer tensor cores can evaluate ciphertext-weight products exactly mod 2^48 in one GEMM. The client evaluates nonlinearities exactly and re-encrypts with fresh secrets, avoiding polynomial approximation or bootstrapping.
AI.result: On 72 windows from 12 bacterial genomes, encryption adds 2.54e-4 nats/token KL divergence (95% CI upper bound 3.95e-4), below a pre-registered non-inferiority margin and indistinguishable from bf16 inference, while the inversion attack drops to chance. A reusable public hint cuts latency 3.54x, wire compression reduces traffic 6.8x, per-layer padding reduces routing leakage from 54.9% to 8.9%, and int4 experts remain non-inferior. Server-side per-expert-token cost is >6 orders of magnitude below a CKKS baseline.
AI.conclusion: CipherGenome enables privacy-preserving inference of large sparse MoE genome models by outsourcing expert computation to untrusted hardware without sacrificing accuracy, offering substantial efficiency gains over CKKS-based approaches.

title: Mirror-Score: Calibrated, Inference-only Scoring Exposes the Limits of Sequence-compatibility Ranking in D-peptide Design
summary: D-peptides combine protease resistance with high target specificity, but computational design of D-peptide binders remains immature. Mirror-Peptidizer introduced an in silico mirror-image screening pipeline using target reflection, backbone generation, and ProteinMPNN sequence design, but its raw ProteinMPNN negative log-likelihood (NLL) ranking was not validated against measured affinities, and only 4 of 9 tested MDM2 designs bound detectably. We introduce Mirror-Score, a calibrated, inference-only scoring framework for heterochiral D-peptide/L-protein complexes, and a public benchmark of 31 crystal complexes across four target families, including 18 with literature-verified affinities. Raw ProteinMPNN NLL is not a valid affinity ranker: its pooled Spearman correlation with affinity is 0.19, and correlations reverse between MDM2/CHIP (+0.62) and gp41 (-0.70). We therefore evaluate Boltz-2 mirror-space cofolding confidence. For the complete viral-entry family (7 structures representing 3 peptides), interface predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT) achieves structure-level leave-one-out Spearman rho = 0.90 (p = 0.006) and correctly orders all three peptides by affinity, whereas NLL fails (structure-level rho = 0.18). Because only three independent chemotypes are represented, this result indicates directional consistency rather than a statistically validated predictor. Cross-family calibration does not transfer at current sample sizes, supporting family-matched calibration as the practical deployment mode. We also specify a prospective design protocol for the antimicrobial-resistance targets LasR and LecB from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, including mirrored structures, ligand-derived hotspot maps, diffusion-model-ready inputs, and Mirror-Score ranking. Code, benchmark data, structures, and analysis scripts are openly available at https://github.com/Jiadalee/Mirror-Score.

AI.tldr: Mirror-Score is a calibrated, inference-only scoring framework for heterochiral D-peptide/L-protein complexes, paired with a 31-structure benchmark. Raw ProteinMPNN NLL fails as an affinity ranker (pooled Spearman 0.19), while Boltz-2 mirror-space interface pLDDT shows directional consistency (viral-entry structure-level rho=0.90), supporting family-matched calibration.
AI.motivation: D-peptides offer protease resistance and high target specificity, but computational design of D-peptide binders is immature. Mirror-Peptidizer's in silico mirror-image pipeline used raw ProteinMPNN NLL ranking without validating it against measured affinities, and only 4 of 9 tested MDM2 designs bound detectably.
AI.method: Mirror-Score: a calibrated, inference-only scoring framework for heterochiral D-peptide/L-protein complexes. Plus a public benchmark of 31 crystal complexes across four target families (18 with literature-verified affinities). The framework evaluates Boltz-2 mirror-space cofolding confidence and uses family-matched calibration; a prospective protocol is specified for LasR and LecB (mirrored structures, ligand-derived hotspot maps, diffusion-model-ready inputs, Mirror-Score ranking).
AI.result: Raw ProteinMPNN NLL is not a valid affinity ranker: pooled Spearman 0.19, with reversed correlations between MDM2/CHIP (+0.62) and gp41 (-0.70). For the viral-entry family (7 structures, 3 peptides), interface pLDDT gives structure-level leave-one-out Spearman rho=0.90 (p=0.006) and orders all three peptides correctly, vs NLL rho=0.18. Cross-family calibration does not transfer at current sample sizes.
AI.conclusion: Interface pLDDT is directionally consistent but not a statistically validated predictor given only three independent chemotypes. Family-matched calibration is the practical deployment mode. Code, benchmark data, structures, and analysis scripts are openly available.

title: Explainability from Training with Applications to TCR-Epitope Prediction
summary: Deep learning models have achieved strong performance in artificial intelligence for science, yet their black-box nature limits our understanding of how they learn scientific tasks. Existing methods for interpretability provide limited insight into how models organize evidence and evolve during learning. We introduce explainability from training (EFT), a model-agnostic paradigm that traces model interpretation during training to explain why models rely on specific features and how they organize these features as predictive evidence. We apply EFT to four state-of-the-art T cell receptor (TCR)-epitope prediction models, TCR-SRIM, TULIP, MixTCRpred, and NetTCR-2.2, spanning post-hoc and interpret-by-design approaches as well as transformers and CNNs. To investigate how structural information affects model explanations, we introduce a benchmark, TCR-XAI2, containing 388 unique experimentally resolved TCR-epitope structures, complemented by structures predicted using AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, TCRModel2, tFold-TCR, and OpenFold3. Using EFT with TCR-XAI2, we demonstrate that (1) CNN and transformer models exhibit distinct learning trajectories; (2) TCR $α$ and $β$ evidence can conflict during learning, limiting the benefits of jointly modeling both chains, while MHC information mitigates this; and (3) real versus predicted structural data for TCR-epitope prediction exhibits distinct TCR and peptide feature preferences as well as differing trajectories of model certainty.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Explainability From Training (EFT), a model-agnostic paradigm that traces how models build interpretations during training. Applied to four TCR-epitope prediction models and a new structural benchmark (TCR-XAI2), it reveals distinct learning trajectories across architectures, conflicting TCR α/β evidence, and differences between real and predicted structural data.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models perform well in AI for science but remain black boxes, limiting understanding of how they learn scientific tasks. Existing interpretability methods give limited insight into how models organize evidence and evolve during learning.
AI.method: EFT, a model-agnostic paradigm tracing model interpretation during training to explain why models rely on specific features and how they organize them as predictive evidence. Applied to four SOTA TCR-epitope models (TCR-SRIM, TULIP, MixTCRpred, NetTCR-2.2), covering post-hoc and interpret-by-design approaches and transformers and CNNs. A new benchmark, TCR-XAI2, includes 388 unique experimentally resolved TCR-epitope structures plus AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, TCRModel2, tFold-TCR, and OpenFold3 predictions.
AI.result: Using EFT with TCR-XAI2, the study shows: (1) CNNs and transformers exhibit distinct learning trajectories; (2) TCR α and β evidence can conflict during learning, limiting benefits of jointly modeling both chains, with MHC information mitigating this; (3) real versus predicted structural data yield distinct TCR and peptide feature preferences and differing trajectories of model certainty.
AI.conclusion: EFT provides a model-agnostic way to trace and explain model interpretation during training, offering new insight into how scientific deep learning models organize evidence. Applying it to TCR-epitope prediction reveals architecture-dependent learning dynamics, chain conflicts, and real-vs-predicted structural effects, highlighting its value for interpretable AI for science.

title: Large-scale factor analysis shows machine intelligence is only partially interpretable
summary: A common assumption in language model development is that cognitive abilities are organized around a general, domain-free intelligence factor, like fluid intelligence in humans. This assumption is rarely tested directly, and prior attempts have done so only at a much smaller scale. We take a latent variable approach to intelligence in language models, similar to how psychometricians study psychological constructs. Performance in every specific problem set is influenced by a domain-specific and a domain-agnostic latent factor. Using factor analysis as a dimension-reduction technique, we analyzed 13,251 published evaluation scores covering 1,618 language models across 456 different text-only benchmarks. Due to the super-sparse nature of the dataset, we triangulate our analysis across different data densifiers and imputation methods. A robust pattern across different modes of bias is that 1. A general intelligence factor accounts for 70.8% of variance in model performance at our most generous estimate, and far less than that in most of our solutions, 2. Content-similar benchmarks do not necessarily cluster together, and 3. The $g$ factor is not dominated by any common theme, and there is a lack of evidence that it is well-proxied by standard "intelligence" benchmarks. Our findings go against current endeavors of defining, identifying, and targeting general intelligence as a tangible construct in language model development. This leaves the strategy of targeting a single conceptual ability without support, since the first-order abilities it would have to reach are often partially idiosyncratic and not identifiable in practice.

AI.tldr: Using factor analysis on 13,251 scores from 1,618 language models across 456 benchmarks, this study tests whether model abilities converge on a single general intelligence factor. A general factor explains 70.8% of variance at most, far less in most solutions, and is not well-proxied by standard "intelligence" benchmarks, undermining the assumption of a domain-free g factor in language models.
AI.motivation: Language model development commonly assumes cognitive abilities are organized around a general, domain-free intelligence factor (like fluid intelligence in humans), but this assumption is rarely tested directly and prior attempts operated at much smaller scales.
AI.method: Adopting a latent variable approach akin to psychometrics, the authors model performance on each problem set as influenced by domain-specific and domain-agnostic latent factors. They apply factor analysis and dimension reduction to 13,251 published evaluation scores covering 1,618 language models across 456 text-only benchmarks, triangulating results across different data densifiers and imputation methods due to the dataset's super-sparse nature.
AI.result: Across modes of bias, the robust pattern is: (1) a general intelligence factor accounts for 70.8% of variance at the most generous estimate, and far less in most solutions; (2) content-similar benchmarks do not necessarily cluster together; (3) the g factor is not dominated by any common theme and lacks evidence of being well-proxied by standard "intelligence" benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The findings challenge efforts to define, identify, and target general intelligence as a tangible construct in language model development, leaving the strategy of targeting a single conceptual ability unsupported, since the first-order abilities it would need to reach are often partially idiosyncratic and not identifiable in practice.

title: Neural Structural Reasoner: A Brain-inspired Architecture for Reasoning over Structured Knowledge
summary: Structural reasoning, the ability to recognize and make inferences over the relational structure between objects and concepts, is a hallmark of human cognition, yet prevailing methods often collapse relational topology into flat embeddings, cannot discover hidden structure and lack interpretability. We introduce Neural Structural Reasoner (NSR), a brain-inspired network that preserves relational structure directly in the connectivity and dynamics of coupled neuronal populations. NSR draws inspiration from three biological mechanisms: multi-layered architecture for encoding hierarchical knowledge, stable representations of entity and concepts, and path integration for input-driven state inference. At query time, NSR parallelizes computation over candidate relational structures and leverages confidence-weighted scores to perform link prediction. Across standard knowledge-graph benchmarks, NSR achieves competitive accuracy without leading on every dataset, and has lower reported training times than several neural baselines. Because reasoning is implemented through sequences of human-readable neuron activations, NSR affords native interpretability by tracking intermediate inference steps. The model further extracts latent relational hierarchies and compositional rules, demonstrating the brain-inspired architecture as an effective, efficient, and highly interpretable substrate for structural reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Neural Structural Reasoner (NSR), a brain-inspired network that encodes relational structure in the connectivity and dynamics of coupled neuronal populations for interpretable structural reasoning and link prediction.
AI.motivation: Structural reasoning is a hallmark of human cognition, but prevailing methods often collapse relational topology into flat embeddings, cannot discover hidden structure, and lack interpretability.
AI.method: NSR draws on three biological mechanisms: a multi-layered architecture for hierarchical knowledge, stable entity/concept representations, and path integration for input-driven state inference. At query time it parallelizes computation over candidate relational structures and uses confidence-weighted scores for link prediction.
AI.result: On standard knowledge-graph benchmarks, NSR achieves competitive accuracy (though not leading on every dataset) with lower reported training times than several neural baselines, and it extracts latent relational hierarchies and compositional rules.
AI.conclusion: The brain-inspired architecture serves as an effective, efficient, and highly interpretable substrate for structural reasoning, with native interpretability via human-readable neuron activation sequences.

title: From Neurons to Conversation: Speech Brain-Computer Interfaces
comment: Review article, 28 pages, 4 figures, 2 boxes, 2 tables
summary: Speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) aim to restore communication by transforming neural activity related to speech, language, or communicative intent into external outputs such as text, synthesized voice, or avatar control. Recent advances in intracortical and electrocorticographic recording, deep sequence models, and language-model-assisted decoding have enabled rapid progress, including high-performance attempted-speech decoding and increasingly naturalistic speech synthesis. Yet these achievements also reveal that speech BCIs are not simply neural-to-text decoders. They are adaptive clinical systems in which neural representations, recording hardware, decoding architectures, language priors, feedback, and user learning interact over time. Here, we synthesize speech BCI research from a system-level perspective. We first examine the neural substrates of speech and language, emphasizing their hierarchical, distributed, temporally structured, and non-stationary organization. We then examine recording and decoding choices, closed-loop adaptation, evaluation, clinical translation, and ethics. Across these domains, we highlight recurring trade-offs between signal resolution and invasiveness, low-level motor and high-level semantic targets, decoder accuracy and user agency, and language-model fluency and faithful neural evidence. We argue the next generation of speech BCIs should be evaluated not only by offline accuracy, but also by robustness across sessions, calibration burden, latency, uncertainty, usability, and safeguards against unintended decoding. By reframing speech BCIs as adaptive, user-centred systems, we outline the interdisciplinary priorities spanning speech neuroscience, neural engineering, machine learning, clinical practice, and neuroethics needed to move from proof-of-concept decoding toward reliable, expressive, and controllable communication neuroprostheses.

However, these achievements reveal that speech BCIs are not merely neural-to-text decoders but adaptive clinical systems where neural representations, hardware, decoding architectures, language priors, feedback, and user learning interact over time. A system-level synthesis is needed to guide the field forward.

The authors first examine the neural substrates of speech and language (hierarchical, distributed, temporally structured, non-stationary organization), then examine recording and decoding choices, closed-loop adaptation, evaluation, clinical translation, and ethics.

Reframing speech BCIs as adaptive, user-centred systems outlines interdisciplinary priorities spanning speech neuroscience, neural engineering, machine learning, clinical practice, and neuroethics to move from proof-of-concept decoding toward reliable, expressive, controllable communication neuroprostheses.

title: Volcanite: Commodity-Hardware Segmentation Volume Visualization for Connectomics and Beyond
summary: Modern imaging produces terabyte-scale segmentation volumes, assigning each voxel an object label. These categorical, boundary-sensitive and label-rich data underpin connectomics and other imaging-driven fields, yet their scale often forces interpretation through slices, approximate meshes or distributed workflows that obscure spatial context and voxel-level defects. Here we show that such volumes can be explored directly on commodity hardware with Volcanite, an open-source framework for dense-segmentation rendering. Combining compression-aware data handling, a Vulkan GPU backend and segmentation-specific rendering, Volcanite enables low-latency exploration without meshing or distributed infrastructure, including for unpublished, sensitive or proprietary data. Across multi-domain datasets, it preserves voxel labels, adds shadows and global illumination, and renders up to half a trillion voxels at 100 frames per second. By replacing lengthy preprocessing with direct inspection, Volcanite decouples hypothesis generation from data preparation and turns teravoxel label fields into interactive evidence for discovery, validation and cross-domain spatial analysis

AI.tldr: Volcanite is an open-source framework that renders terabyte-scale dense segmentation volumes directly on commodity hardware, avoiding meshing or distributed infrastructure and achieving up to 100 fps on half a trillion voxels.
AI.motivation: Modern imaging yields terabyte-scale segmentation volumes with voxel-level object labels, critical for connectomics and other fields. Their scale currently forces interpretation via slices, approximate meshes, or distributed workflows that lose spatial context and hide voxel-level defects.
AI.method: Volcanite combines compression-aware data handling, a Vulkan GPU backend, and segmentation-specific rendering to enable low-latency, direct exploration of dense-segmentation volumes without meshing or distributed infrastructure, working on unpublished, sensitive, or proprietary data.
AI.result: Across multi-domain datasets, it preserves voxel labels, adds shadows and global illumination, and renders up to half a trillion voxels at 100 frames per second on commodity hardware.
AI.conclusion: By replacing lengthy preprocessing with direct inspection, Volcanite decouples hypothesis generation from data preparation and turns teravoxel label fields into interactive evidence for discovery, validation, and cross-domain spatial analysis.

title: Scalable Diffusion SBI for Compositional Inference under Simulator Misspecification
summary: Simulation-based inference is challenging when many heterogeneous observations must be composed, hierarchical latent structure must be preserved, and the simulator is misspecified relative to observed data. We develop sampling and fine-tuning methods for diffusion-based inference in design-conditional settings, where the same simulator is queried across different experimental conditions $ξ$. We extend compositional score-based inference with a continuous-time diffusion coefficient that accounts for the number of observations, avoiding Jacobian and auxiliary-covariance corrections. We introduce Hierarchical Blockwise Diffusion Sampling (HBDS), which infers shared parameters and group-specific latent states using a single pretrained model, with the hierarchy specified only at sampling time. Together, these methods support variable observation sets and groupings without retraining. To address misspecification, we introduce path-regularized fine-tuning that adapts the learned likelihood to observations and transfers corrections to posterior inference. Using Girsanov's theorem, we quantify path divergence between pretrained and fine-tuned models across experimental designs and interpret it alongside predictive errors to distinguish candidate misspecification correction from unnecessary adaptation. We evaluate compositional sampling on exact-score Gaussian and Simple Likelihood, Complex Posterior benchmarks, HBDS with analytic and learned scores on a controlled hierarchical model, and fine-tuning and localization on a separate analytic model with known design-dependent discrepancy. Finally, we apply the framework to 940 measurements across four cell lines in a mechanistic Bone Morphogenetic Protein signaling model, where fine-tuning improves posterior-predictive accuracy relative to the pretrained model and shifts posterior marginals toward the least-squares reference while retaining spread.

AI.tldr: The paper develops diffusion-based sampling and fine-tuning methods for design-conditional simulation-based inference under compositional observations, hierarchical latents, and simulator misspecification.
AI.motivation: Simulation-based inference struggles when many heterogeneous observations must be composed, hierarchical latent structure must be preserved, and the simulator is misspecified relative to real data.
AI.method: Extends compositional score-based inference with a continuous-time diffusion coefficient scaling with observation count (avoiding Jacobian/auxiliary-covariance corrections); introduces Hierarchical Blockwise Diffusion Sampling (HBDS) to infer shared and group-specific latents with a single pretrained model, hierarchy specified only at sampling; adds path-regularized fine-tuning, using Girsanov's theorem to quantify path divergence.
AI.result: Evaluated on Gaussian/Simple Likelihood/Complex Posterior benchmarks, HBDS on a hierarchical model, and fine-tuning on an analytic model with known discrepancy; applied to 940 measurements across four cell lines in a BMP signaling model, where fine-tuning improved posterior-predictive accuracy and shifted marginals toward least-squares reference while retaining spread.
AI.conclusion: The framework supports variable observation sets and groupings without retraining and enables principled misspecification correction, distinguishing genuine corrections from unnecessary adaptation.

title: AssayRouter: Historical Utility Priors for Frozen Molecular Predictor Routing
summary: Laboratories often face a new molecular assay with 16-64 labels and a bank of predictors whose training data and parameters are unavailable. The practical question is which frozen outputs to include in a small local model. AssayRouter treats completed assays as pseudo-targets and labels each candidate by its post-fit utility: the reduction in held-out discovery loss when the candidate is added to the local target predictor. A shared regressor learns to predict this utility from candidate behavior on the support set, without source identity; on a new assay, one frozen ranking selects four sources and separate labels fit a convex combiner. We train only on completed ChEMBL-MT assays and evaluate 24 external regression assays across six frozen interface families. AssayRouter-C lowers strict four-call negative log-likelihood (NLL) by 0.0409 relative to Support-CV@4. Frozen candidate-label permutations confirm that candidate-utility correspondence carries the transferred information, and leave-one-interface-out training shows that the mapping generalizes to unseen predictor families. Completed assays therefore provide transferable supervision for scarce-label routing through frozen prediction interfaces.

AI.tldr: AssayRouter selects which frozen predictors to include in a small local model for new assays with 16-64 labels, using completed assays as pseudo-targets to learn candidate selection utility.
AI.motivation: Laboratories often face new molecular assays with only 16-64 labels and a bank of frozen predictors whose training data and parameters are unavailable. The practical challenge is deciding which frozen outputs to include in a small local model.
AI.method: AssayRouter treats completed assays as pseudo-targets and labels each candidate by its post-fit utility, i.e., the reduction in held-out discovery loss when the candidate is added to the local predictor. A shared regressor predicts this utility from candidate support-set behavior without source identity. On a new assay, one frozen ranking selects four sources and separate labels fit a convex combiner.
AI.result: Trained only on completed ChEMBL-MT assays and evaluated on 24 external regression assays across six frozen interface families, AssayRouter-C lowers strict four-call NLL by 0.0409 versus Support-CV@4. Frozen candidate-label permutations confirm candidate-utility correspondence carries the transferred information, and leave-one-interface-out training shows generalization to unseen predictor families.
AI.conclusion: Completed assays provide transferable supervision for scarce-label routing through frozen prediction interfaces.

title: Benchmarking graph-based models for in-silico toxicity prediction in drug discovery
summary:
Drug discovery is a costly and high-risk process, where toxicity-related failures remain a major cause of attrition in both preclinical and clinical stages. As a result, accurate early prediction of chemical toxicity is essential to reduce downstream costs and improve compound prioritization. In this context, graph deep learning (GDL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for toxicity prediction, leveraging molecular graph representations to learn directly from chemical structure with improved expressivity over traditional approaches.
  Despite the growing number of proposed models, current literature-based comparisons are often difficult to interpret due to inconsistencies in datasets, preprocessing pipelines, and evaluation protocols. To address this limitation, we introduce a unified and standardized benchmarking framework for GDL-based toxicity prediction. We systematically evaluate more than 20 representative approaches under consistent experimental conditions and across multiple datasets and partitioning strategies, enabling a fair and reproducible comparison of model performance. In addition, we complement this empirical study with a structured literature analysis to contextualize existing methodological trends and performance claims. Our results provide a clearer and more reliable assessment of the current state of the field, highlighting both the strengths and limitations of existing graph-based approaches. To support transparency and reproducibility, we release our benchmarking framework as open-source software https://gitlab.citius.gal/noel.suarez/benchtox, allowing the community to evaluate and compare models under consistent conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces BenchTox, a unified open-source benchmarking framework for graph deep learning (GDL)-based chemical toxicity prediction, evaluating 20+ representative models under standardized conditions to enable fair, reproducible comparisons.
AI.motivation: Toxicity-related failures are a major cause of attrition in drug discovery, making accurate early toxicity prediction critical for reducing costs and improving compound prioritization. GDL has emerged as a powerful paradigm for this task, but literature-based comparisons are hard to interpret due to inconsistencies in datasets, preprocessing, and evaluation protocols.
AI.method: The authors build a unified, standardized benchmarking framework for GDL-based toxicity prediction. They systematically evaluate more than 20 representative approaches under consistent experimental conditions across multiple datasets and partitioning strategies, and complement the empirical study with a structured literature analysis of methodological trends and performance claims.
AI.result: The framework provides a clearer and more reliable assessment of the field's current state, highlighting strengths and limitations of existing graph-based approaches under fair, reproducible conditions.
AI.conclusion: The work addresses comparability issues in GDL toxicity prediction and releases the BenchTox framework as open-source software (https://gitlab.citius.gal/noel.suarez/benchtox) to support transparency, reproducibility, and consistent community benchmarking.

title: Flattening the Connectome Spectrum: A Spectral Filter for FC Induces a Pretraining Target for fMRI Encoders
summary: Self-supervised pretraining reshaped prediction in language and vision, and brain foundation models (BFMs) inherited its promise. Representations learned from large unlabelled corpora should capture individual functional dynamics and generalise across cohorts. However, kernel ridge regression (KRR) fitted on functional connectivity (FC) matrices still predicts individual phenotypes more accurately than any BFM we tested. In this paper, we show that KRR is weighted by the eigenvalues of the FC which are miscalibrated for phenotype prediction. We apply an efficient spectral filter to recalibrate the eigenvalues of each subject's FC matrix, enabling the model to exploit more inter-individual variance. Across the 5 datasets, 11 parcellations and 6 prediction targets we tested, we match or exceed the KRR baseline. Based on this finding, we then pretrain a small encoder model on about 4,000 hours of fMRI from 162 open datasets, whereby we align the pairwise similarities between the embeddings of recording snippets with those between the recalibrated connectomes. Our model performs on par with the best of the 6 published BFMs we tested while having an order of magnitude fewer parameters. Our encoder performs better than FC on short scans and in smaller cohorts, especially in fingerprinting. We release the pretrained model weights, the code and the pretraining data, preprocessed and parcellated.

AI.tldr: This paper shows kernel ridge regression (KRR) on functional connectivity is limited by miscalibrated eigenvalues, and fixes this with a spectral filter. The authors then pretrain a small encoder aligned to recalibrated connectomes, matching top brain foundation models with far fewer parameters.
AI.motivation: Brain foundation models promise to capture individual functional dynamics and generalize across cohorts, but KRR on functional connectivity matrices still predicts phenotypes more accurately than any tested BFM. The authors investigate why and aim to close this gap.
AI.method: The authors identify that KRR is weighted by FC eigenvalues that are miscalibrated for phenotype prediction. They apply an efficient spectral filter to recalibrate each subject's FC eigenvalues, then pretrain a small encoder on ~4,000 hours of fMRI from 162 open datasets, aligning pairwise embedding similarities with those of the recalibrated connectomes.
AI.result: Across 5 datasets, 11 parcellations, and 6 prediction targets, the method matches or exceeds the KRR baseline, especially on short scans, smaller cohorts, and fingerprinting. The encoder performs on par with the best of 6 published BFMs while using an order of magnitude fewer parameters.
AI.conclusion: Recalibrating FC eigenvalues via spectral filtering explains KRR's strength and yields a compact, well-performing brain encoder. The authors release pretrained weights, code, and preprocessed pretraining data.

title: LEMON-ZEST: Evolution-Informed Tokenization for Efficient Protein Language Modeling
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. 9 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: Protein Language Models (PLMs) have made remarkable progress following scaling laws established in natural language processing across sequence- and structure-based tasks, yet the potential of tokenization remains underexploited. Unlike human language, proteins preserve structure despite extensive sequence variation a property standard tokenization strategies fundamentally fail to capture. We introduce ZEST (Zoned Encoding of Sequence Traits), an evolution-informed vocabulary derived from conserved regions of multiple sequence alignments. ZEST allows embedding domain-level biological priors directly at the tokenization stage rather than learning them implicitly through scale. ZEST natively compresses sequences to an average token length of 4 residues, enabling our model to process 4,000 residues within a standard 1024-token context window. Building on this, we present LEMON (Layered Extraction of Molecular Ordering from Nature), a compact 200M-parameter sequence-based model for detection of remote homology between protein sequences trained on a single H100 GPU for one week. Despite its modest size, LEMON outperforms state-of-the-art models ranging from 600M to 3B parameters. Our results demonstrate that evolution-informed tokenization can substitute for massive parameter scaling, opening a new direction for efficient, biologically-grounded protein representation learning. All code, model weights, and results are publicly available under the MIT license.

AI.tldr: ZEST is an evolution-informed tokenization scheme based on conserved MSA regions that compresses proteins to ~4 residues per token, and LEMON (200M params) outperforms 600M-3B models on remote homology detection.
AI.motivation: PLMs follow scaling laws from NLP, but tokenization for proteins is underexploited. Unlike human language, proteins preserve structure despite extensive sequence variation, a property standard tokenization fails to capture.
AI.method: ZEST (Zoned Encoding of Sequence Traits): a vocabulary derived from conserved regions of multiple sequence alignments, embedding domain-level biological priors at tokenization. It compresses sequences to avg 4 residues/token, fitting 4,000 residues in a 1024-token context. LEMON is a 200M-param sequence model for remote homology detection, trained on one H100 GPU for one week.
AI.result: Despite modest size, LEMON outperforms state-of-the-art models ranging from 600M to 3B parameters.
AI.conclusion: Evolution-informed tokenization can substitute for massive parameter scaling, opening a new direction for efficient, biologically-grounded protein representation learning. Code, weights, and results are public under MIT license.

title: OmniVCBench: Benchmarking Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Reasoning Towards AI Virtual Cells
summary: Artificial Intelligence Virtual Cells (AIVCs) are envisioned as scientific agents that simulate cellular responses, explain underlying mechanisms, and support hypothesis-driven discovery. Existing AIVC benchmarks, however, operate primarily at the simulation layer, motivating complementary evaluation of how models interpret experimental evidence and formulate biological hypotheses. We introduce OmniVCBench, a figure-centric, source-traceable benchmark for the interpretation component of an AIVC. It contains 6,077 curated single- and multi-subfigure question--answer pairs derived from figures and experimental contexts in the scientific literature. Guided by Bloom's taxonomy, we instantiate interpretation-layer counterparts of the AIVC Predict--Explain--Discover agenda through three scientific reasoning tasks. We further introduce AIVC-Judge, a task-conditioned MLLM-as-a-judge framework with category-specific, reference-aware rubrics for evaluating open-ended responses. A complementary Model-Derived Hard-Negative Mining (MDHNM) strategy converts plausible errors observed during model inference into MCQ distractors for lower-cost evaluation. Within the evaluated heterogeneous model pool, MCQ accuracy correlates positively with AIVC-Judge scores, providing a complementary view of performance alongside open-response evaluation. Code and data demo are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OmniVCBench.

AI.tldr: OmniVCBench is a figure-centric, source-traceable benchmark for the interpretation layer of AI Virtual Cells, with 6,077 QA pairs across three reasoning tasks, plus an MLLM-as-a-judge framework (AIVC-Judge) and a hard-negative mining strategy.
AI.motivation: Existing AIVC benchmarks operate mainly at the simulation layer, leaving the interpretation layer—how models interpret experimental evidence and formulate biological hypotheses—under-evaluated.
AI.method: Curated 6,077 single- and multi-subfigure QA pairs from literature figures, organized via Bloom's taxonomy into three interpretation-layer tasks (Predict-Explain-Discover counterparts), evaluated with AIVC-Judge (task-conditioned, reference-aware rubrics) and MDHNM that converts model errors into MCQ distractors.
AI.result: MCQ accuracy correlates positively with AIVC-Judge scores across the heterogeneous model pool, offering complementary views of performance.
AI.conclusion: OmniVCBench provides a complementary interpretation-layer evaluation for AIVCs, combining open-ended judging and low-cost MCQ evaluation.

title: 2-Dimensional spectral gating for denoising bioacoustics recordings
summary: Isolating vocalizations from noise in bioacoustics recordings is a prerequisite to many ecological analyses, including species identification, animal communication understanding, and individual or population-level variability studies. However, when recordings are acquired in open environments, vocalizations, noise, or signal-to-noise ratio can vary widely across individuals, species, environment, and recording conditions, making it hard to develop robust and generalizable methods for ecological analyses. To account for these challenges, noise reduction techniques are used to remove noise before downstream analyses. Popular methods such as Noisereduce rely on spectral gating, which estimates a noise threshold for each frequency channel. We propose a further improvement to Noisereduce, leveraging the fact that most animal sounds have structure across multiple frequencies. We apply our method on bird and marine mammals recordings and show that our extension of Noisereduce leads to improved denoising in both above and under water acoustic recordings, without impacting speed of preprocessing.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an enhancement to Noisereduce's spectral gating denoising method by exploiting the multi-frequency structure of animal sounds, improving denoising for bird and marine mammal recordings without slowing preprocessing.
AI.motivation: Isolating vocalizations from noise is essential for ecological analyses (species ID, communication studies, variability studies), but varying noise and SNR across individuals, species, environments, and recording conditions make robust, generalizable methods hard. Noise reduction is thus applied before downstream analyses.
AI.method: The authors extend Noisereduce, a popular spectral gating method that estimates a noise threshold per frequency channel, by leveraging the fact that most animal sounds have structure across multiple frequencies.
AI.result: Applied to bird and marine mammal recordings, the extension improves denoising in both above-water and underwater acoustic recordings, without impacting preprocessing speed.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-frequency-aware extension of Noisereduce provides more effective denoising across diverse acoustic recording conditions while maintaining computational efficiency.

title: Which Attention Heads are like the Human Head? Not the Ones that Compute
summary: Brain-AI alignment is often interpreted as a sign that model and brain perform similar computations. Whether the aligned units are causally involved in model computation is rarely checked. On an abstract pattern-completion task (AAABAAA $\rightarrow$ B), we compare LLM attention-head representations with human EEG and test how ablating those heads affects task performance. Alignment and causation dissociate: brain-aligned heads contribute to performance, but their removal is substantially less disruptive than removal of heads selected via attribution patching. We compare two head sets that prior interpretability work defines without reference to the brain: concept vectors (CVs), which represent abstract patterns across formats, and function vectors (FVs), selected for their contribution to correct-answer prediction. Brain alignment shows little association with FV scores, while its association with CV scores varies across models. Among brain-aligned heads, we find recurring attention profiles: one emphasizes distinctive elements (novelty heads), the other repeating elements (repetition heads). The novelty family tracks salience and attends to the same elements that humans look at, yet its removal is less damaging than random ablation on average. Repetition heads contribute modestly to performance and are associated with abstract-pattern representation (CVs). Across 17 models spanning 3B-72B parameters, FV-ranked removal is substantially more disruptive than brain-ranked removal. Brain alignment thus captures how the model reads the stimulus, and only faintly captures how it represents the pattern and solves the task.

AI.tldr: Brain-AI alignment reflects how models read stimuli, not the causal computation behind task solving.
AI.motivation: Alignment is often taken as evidence that model and brain perform similar computations, but whether aligned units are causally involved in model computation is rarely verified.
AI.method: On an abstract pattern-completion task (AAABAAA → B), the authors compare LLM attention-head representations with human EEG and ablate aligned heads. They contrast brain-aligned heads with heads from concept vectors (CVs) and function vectors (FVs), and analyze attention profiles across 17 models (3B-72B).
AI.result: Alignment and causation dissociate: brain-aligned heads contribute to performance but their removal is far less disruptive than FV-ranked ablation. Brain alignment shows little link to FV scores, variable link to CV scores. Two recurrent profiles emerge: novelty heads (salience, human-like attention, low damage) and repetition heads (modest contribution, linked to CVs). FV-ranked removal is consistently more disruptive than brain-ranked removal.
AI.conclusion: Brain alignment captures how the model reads the stimulus, but only faintly captures how it represents the pattern and solves the task.

title: Traversing the solution space of neural networks with Hessian Null Space Continuation
comment: 55 pages, 39 figures. Project page and code: https://ann-huang-0.github.io/Hessian-null-space-continuation/
summary: On a single task, deep networks can learn many solutions, depending on their optimizer, training data, architecture, and hyperparameters. Many of these solutions are mode-connected: rather than isolated points in weight space, they are connected by low-loss regions. Yet how their internal computation varies within these regions is unknown. A parallel line of work has identified the degeneracy of neural representations: many networks reach similar training loss with distinct internal structures. However, it is unclear how these solutions are related in weight space. We unify these subfields and show for the first time that many different internal mechanisms exist within a local mode-connected region in weight space. To do so, we introduce Hessian Null Space Continuation (HNC), a scalable method that uses local curvature to traverse regions of weight space that preserve network function, and can be steered toward solutions with specified properties. In RNNs trained on a memory task, HNC reaches drastically different representations and dynamics with maintained behavior. In ImageNet-trained Vision Transformers, HNC finds representations that differ more from the original network than any independently trained model with a different architecture or objective. In reinforcement-learning agents, HNC uncovers a distinct navigation strategy at comparable return and exposes reward hacking in an AI Safety Gridworld. Finally, HNC measures the local geometry of the solution set, showing how model size and task complexity shape its dimension and functional sensitivity. Our results show that a surprisingly large amount of representational diversity exists near a single trained solution, unseen by standard gradient-based optimization. HNC identifies and quantifies this diversity, opening new possibilities for mechanistic understanding of solution spaces and for model merging, editing, and fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Deep networks contain many mode-connected solutions connected by low-loss regions, but how internal computation varies within these regions was unknown. The authors introduce Hessian Null Space Continuation (HNC), which traverses weight space while preserving function, revealing large representational diversity near a single trained solution.
AI.motivation: Prior work shows solutions are mode-connected within low-loss regions, and separately that neural representations are degenerate (different internals, similar loss). However, it was unclear how these distinct internal mechanisms relate in weight space and whether varied representations exist within a single mode-connected region.
AI.method: HNC (Hessian Null Space Continuation): a scalable method that uses local curvature to traverse weight-space regions preserving network function, and can be steered toward solutions with specified properties.
AI.result: In RNNs on a memory task, HNC reaches very different representations/dynamics with maintained behavior. In ImageNet ViTs, HNC finds representations differing more from the original than any independently trained model with a different architecture or objective. In RL agents, HNC uncovers a distinct navigation strategy at comparable return and exposes reward hacking in an AI Safety Gridworld. HNC also measures solution-set geometry, showing how model size and task complexity shape its dimension and functional sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: Surprisingly large representational diversity exists near a single trained solution, unseen by standard gradient-based optimization. HNC identifies and quantifies this diversity, opening possibilities for mechanistic understanding of solution spaces and for model merging, editing, and fine-tuning.
